name: Real-time personalization / ranking & recsys features (live commerce, marketplace ranking)
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: Real-time personalization, marketplace ranking, and recsys feature serving (feed ranking, search ranking, live-commerce show ranking, recently-viewed-items, in-session affinity)
domain_fit.one_line_definition: A ranking service must score hundreds of candidate items per user request inside a ~100–200 ms end-to-end budget, using per-user, per-item, and per-(user, item-attribute) behavioural features that are fresh to the current session.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: Three concrete jobs: (1) Serve a per-request batched read of behavioural features for the ~100–500 candidate items going into a ranking model (XGBoost/LightGBM, two-tower retrieval scorer, or a transformer/cross-encoder re-ranker), so the second-stage ranker can fold in per-item rolling popularity, per-(user, category) affinity, and per-(user, seller) trust without blowing the request budget — Tecton, Chalk, Hopsworks, Feast and Fennel all motivate themselves on exactly this 'feature fan-out at ranking time' problem. (2) Maintain in-session signals (last-N items viewed / dwelled / favorited / added-to-cart / purchased, items shown but not clicked, current dwell distribution) so the ranker reacts within the same session and not the next day's batch; this is the freshness wedge live-commerce platforms (Whatnot, TikTok Shop) cite as the reason batch features are obsolete for them. (3) Maintain per-item rolling popularity / velocity (views/min, clicks/min, CTR, add-to-cart rate, watch-time distribution) so freshly-introduced items (newly-launched livestreams, flash-sale SKUs, just-listed marketplace items) get a cold-start signal in seconds rather than after the next batch run.
domain_fit.event_shapes: Typical events that would land in beava as @bv.event records: page_view {ts, user_id, item_id, surface, dwell_ms, position}, impression {ts, user_id, item_id, surface, position, query?}, click {ts, user_id, item_id, surface, position}, add_to_cart {ts, user_id, sku, price, qty}, favorite / save {ts, user_id, item_id}, purchase {ts, user_id, order_id, sku, price, qty, seller_id, category, brand}, livestream_join / leave {ts, user_id, show_id, seller_id}, livestream_dwell {ts, user_id, show_id, duration_ms}, chat_message {ts, user_id, show_id}, query {ts, user_id, q_hash, results_returned}, item_listed / item_updated {ts, item_id, seller_id, category, price}. Most identifiers are stable opaque IDs (user_id, item_id, seller_id, show_id, sku, category_id, brand_id); the repo's existing python/beava/demos/ecommerce/ demo already ships PageView / AddToCart / Purchase records keyed on user_id and sku.
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Per-entity aggregations expressed as beava @bv.table primitives. By entity: user_id → last_n(item_id, n=50) for last-viewed / last-clicked / last-purchased streams, count(click, 1m/10m/1h/24h), count(add_to_cart, 24h), n_unique(category, 24h/7d), distribution(dwell_ms, 1h), sum(purchase_amount, 24h/7d), velocity(click, 1m); item_id → count(impression, 1m/10m/1h), count(click, 1m/10m/1h), CTR = clicks/impressions rolling, count(add_to_cart, 1h), count(purchase, 1h/24h), distribution(dwell_ms, 1h), n_unique(user_id, 1h) as 'unique viewers'; (user_id, category) → count(click, 7d/30d), affinity score (clicks/total), recency-decayed dwell sum, time-since-last-interaction; (user_id, seller_id) → count(purchase, 90d), count(view, 30d), repeat-purchase rate; show_id (livestream) → count(join, 1m), distribution(dwell_ms, current-session), n_unique(user_id, 1m), velocity(chat, 1m). Both exact (counters, sums, last-N) and approximate (HLL for unique-viewer counts at high cardinality, distributions for dwell histograms) aggregates have legitimate roles; the ranking model rarely needs accounting-grade exactness.
domain_fit.entity_grain: Mixed and parallel. Primary keys in production ranking rigs include: user_id, item_id (SKU, show_id, listing_id), seller_id / creator_id, category_id, brand_id, (user_id, category_id) pair, (user_id, seller_id) pair, (user_id, brand_id) pair, query_hash, session_id. A single ranking call reads features for one user_id and a fan-out of N item_ids plus the corresponding (user, category) / (user, seller) pairs.
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: Sliding windows dominate for user-side recency (1m, 5m, 1h, 24h, 7d, 30d) and for item-side popularity (1m, 10m, 1h). Session windows are critical for live commerce and clickstream re-ranking (per livestream session, per browse session). Tumbling windows show up for daily/hourly business reporting and for offline-online consistency checks (Hopsworks / Tecton both emphasize point-in-time correctness for training-serving parity). Exactness is largely NOT required for the ranker — ranking models are robust to 1–2 % HLL/CMS error on high-cardinality grains (per-item unique viewers, per-IP fanout) and that error is invisible compared to model variance. Exactness IS desired for the offline materialization that produces training labels.
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: At-least-once with idempotent counters (key = event_id or (user_id, item_id, ts) tuple) is sufficient for the auth-time ranking path; a duplicate-counted click does not change the score appreciably. Strict no-double-count is not required at ranking time.

technical_fit.latency_budget: End-to-end ranking budget is typically 100–200 ms (Netflix cites sub-100 ms recommendation latency at global scale; Whatnot on Chalk reports ~100 ms P99 and ~150 ms end-to-end including 1 MB+ payloads with tens of thousands of features; Apartment List on Chalk targets sub-5 ms per-feature retrieval). The feature fetch sub-budget is usually 5–30 ms because the model inference itself takes 30–80 ms. Beava's published sub-millisecond TCP get / batch_get sits comfortably inside the feature-fetch sub-budget; the open question is the batch_get fan-out shape (one call returning ~30–50 features × ~200 candidates).
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Seconds for in-session signals (last-viewed, current-dwell, just-clicked) — Whatnot, TikTok Shop, and Instacart all cite multi-minute lag as the failure mode that motivates real-time feature stores. Sub-minute for per-item rolling popularity in live commerce (new shows trend in seconds). Minutes-to-hours is acceptable for slower aggregates (7-day category affinity). Beava's push-on-event model gives single-digit-ms feature staleness and fits the strictest tier.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Read-dominated and highly bursty. A single ranking call multiplies into a read fan-out of 100–500 batched feature lookups. Typical mid-size marketplace QPS is 1k–10k ranking requests/sec, which lands at 100k–5M feature reads/sec. DoorDash documents >1M predictions/sec on their store-ranking system and >20M feature reads/sec on their internal feature store. Whatnot via Chalk reports 300M+ features/sec across the platform. Beava's published 684k EPS on a single Apple-M4 core sits at the high end of mid-tier needs but is well below DoorDash / Chalk-class production tiers (those run multi-node sharded Redis or Aerospike clusters), so single-node beava fits a single mid-sized buyer but not a global platform. [uncertain] beava's published read-throughput numbers for batch_get with high candidate fan-out — the 684k EPS figure is the write-side ingest number.
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Strongly read-heavy at ranking time (often 10:1 to 100:1 read:write), inverted from fraud/ad-tech. This is the canonical 'feature-store fan-out at ranking' shape: one user event triggers one or a few writes, but each ranking decision triggers dozens-to-hundreds of batched reads. DoorDash and Tecton both call this out as a critical sizing factor.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Order-of-magnitude per buyer: a mid-sized marketplace with ~10M MAU × ~5 grains (user, item, (user, category), (user, seller), session) × ~30–80 features × ~16–64 bytes per counter (more for last-N item lists and distributions) ≈ 50–200 GB hot state, near the upper edge of a single beava box. A large global marketplace (Whatnot-class with hundreds of millions of impressions/day, Pinterest, DoorDash) pushes into the multi-TB range with billions of (user, item) pairs and exceeds the single-binary in-memory ceiling. Beava's in-memory-only model fits the long-tail of mid-sized marketplaces but not the head-tier.
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Slowly-growing on user_id (MAU), bounded-ish on category_id / brand_id / seller_id, explosive and unbounded on item_id (SKU, listing, livestream show — millions to billions of items; user×item pair grain is the cardinality killer). Last-N item lists per user are O(N) per user which is bounded; (user, item) pair features are NOT typically materialized — they are computed at request time from user-side and item-side features. Eviction / TTL story matters a lot here.
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Mixed TTLs. In-session last-N lists: minutes-to-hours. Per-user behavioural profile: 30–90 days (rolling). Long-term affinity: 6–12 months. Per-item popularity: 1m–24h rolling. Live-commerce show stats: lifetime of the show (minutes-to-hours) and then archived. Cold storage of (user, item) interaction logs for training data: years, in a warehouse — not in beava.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: Highly fan-out: 5–30 user-side features × 1 user + 10–50 per-item features × 100–500 candidates + 5–10 contextual features. Total feature reads per ranking call: ~1,000–25,000. Whatnot on Chalk reports payloads exceeding 1 MB with 'tens of thousands of features' per ranking request. This is the shape beava's batch_get must support efficiently; it is qualitatively different from the fraud-domain shape (one decision, 20–100 features).
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Best-effort to crash-safe. Loss of recent in-session signals during a crash is recoverable (the session itself usually short-circuits) and the long-term aggregates are typically replayed from a warehouse / Kafka archive. Regulator-grade durability is NOT required for ranking. Beava's WAL + periodic snapshot is more than sufficient for this domain.
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Single-binary regional fits a single-region marketplace, a mid-sized e-commerce ranking team, or a single-tenant SaaS personalization product cleanly. Multi-region active-active for global marketplaces is NOT supported in beava v0 — no in-process sharding, no cross-region replication. Buyers running a Whatnot-class global live-commerce platform would need an external sharding / replication layer or a multi-node successor.

commercial_fit.who_buys: Primarily the ML platform / personalization-infra team (Head of ML Platform, Director of Search & Recommendations, Staff ML Eng) at marketplaces, live-commerce platforms, content platforms, e-commerce retailers, news / media apps. Secondary buyer: the growth / experimentation team that owns the feed and ranking experiments. Tertiary: the data platform team that owns the upstream event bus.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: Large and growing. Real-time-feature-store and online-inference vendors raised significant rounds (Tecton, Chalk, Hopsworks, Fennel — Fennel acquired by Databricks in 2025/2026). DoorDash, Instacart, Whatnot, Apartment List, Sony PlayStation are public references for real-time feature serving on Redis / Aerospike / Chalk / internal stacks. Livestream commerce alone is a fast-growing segment: TikTok Shop drove >$100M U.S. sales on Black Friday 2024 across >30k livestream sessions; Whatnot reports >$3B in live sales in the year prior to the Chalk case study; the livestream-ecommerce market is projected at ~33.9 % CAGR. The horizontal recsys / personalization spend is much larger — Netflix attributes 80 %+ of watch time to recommendations, YouTube 70 %, Spotify 60 %. [uncertain] precise revenue figures for Tecton / Chalk / Fennel — most are private.
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: Three forces: (1) Freshness gap — batch-trained models updated daily are obviously stale for live commerce (a livestream that started 60 seconds ago has zero batch features) and increasingly stale even for traditional e-commerce as session-level personalization becomes table stakes. (2) Compute economics — running a 'compute everything in Spark at request time' architecture is uneconomic; collapsing it to a pushed-counter feature server is materially cheaper. (3) Org pull from cross-functional ML platform teams — DoorDash, Instacart, Whatnot have all publicly justified building / buying real-time feature platforms in the past 2–3 years, which gives buyers internal precedent.
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: Light. GDPR / CCPA apply because user_id / session_id / device_id are personal data; right-to-erasure requires being able to delete per-user state on demand (which beava's per-entity TTL story supports). EU DSA / DMA increasingly require ranking-transparency for very large platforms but the constraint lands on documentation, not feature storage. No PCI / AML / FFIEC / HIPAA exposure typically. SOC 2 Type II is table stakes for the buyer's enterprise customers.
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: A runnable per-user last-N-viewed-SKU and per-item rolling-CTR demo can stand up in roughly a day on beava: the repo already ships python/beava/demos/ecommerce/ with PageView / AddToCart / Purchase events keyed on user_id and sku, which is exactly the recsys event shape. A realistic 30–80-feature per-user / per-item / per-(user, category) ranking-feature rig integrated against a real impression / click stream is typically a 1–2 week effort; replicating a Whatnot-class production ranking platform is a multi-quarter project even with beava as the substrate.

competition.incumbents: Two layers. (a) Generic real-time feature stores: Tecton (real-time serving + Spark/Flink materialization), Chalk (real-time feature engine, the Whatnot reference customer, 300M+ features/sec, sub-150 ms ranking), Hopsworks (RonDB-backed feature store with published benchmarks), Feast (open-source, typically on Redis), Fennel (Rust-based, ex-Facebook, acquired by Databricks), Featureform (virtual feature store), AWS SageMaker Feature Store. (b) Online stores used to build feature stores in-house: Redis / managed Redis, Aerospike (Sony PlayStation, Adobe, Criteo, Wayfair public references), DynamoDB, RocksDB, Cassandra. (c) Ranking-service products: Metarank (open-source learn-to-rank with Redis state, 10–20 ms reranking p99), Recombee, Algolia AI Recommendations, Amazon Personalize. Beava competes most directly with the (Redis or Aerospike) + (Flink or Spark Real-Time Mode) two-box pattern, by collapsing it into a single binary.
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: Domain-specific personalization platforms that buyers would otherwise procure as black boxes: Dynamic Yield, Adobe Target, Algolia AI Recommendations, Bloomreach, Recombee, Amazon Personalize, Google Recommendations AI, Coveo, Constructor.io. Beava is not directly competing with these — it is the infrastructure layer a buyer who is building their own ranking stack would use.
competition.beava_differentiator: Five concrete differentiators relevant to recsys ranking: (1) Single binary — no Kafka + Flink + Redis + feature-store ETL chain; lower ops surface area for ML platform teams that don't want to run a streaming engine. (2) 50+ first-class aggregation primitives — counters, velocities, distributions, last-N lists, rates — which is exactly the shape of features ranking teams build on top of Redis Lua / Aerospike UDFs. (3) Push-on-event ingestion (HTTP/JSON, framed TCP, msgpack) avoids the Kafka-only assumption of Tecton/Feast/Hopsworks pipelines; many marketplace event streams are already HTTP webhooks or mobile-SDK direct push. (4) Apache-2.0, no open-core split — buyer is not negotiating against a paid Enterprise Edition. (5) batch_get / get-many semantics map naturally to the ranking fan-out (one call, many features, many entities) — though the read-amplification at 100–500 candidate × 30 features still needs to be validated against beava's published numbers.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: Concrete gaps that will block production ranking deployments today: (1) No TLS / no auth on :8080/:8081/:8090 — ML platform teams running on cloud VPCs will demand mTLS or at minimum bearer-token auth before letting beava sit next to a ranking service. (2) No in-process sharding — Whatnot / DoorDash / Instacart-class state cannot fit on one machine; vertical scaling only. (3) No cross-region replication — global marketplaces with multi-region ranking paths cannot use beava as the source of truth. (4) Read-amplification story for batch_get with 100–500 candidate fan-out × 30 features per item is unproven publicly; the headline 684k EPS is the write-side number. (5) No vector / ANN index — modern two-tower retrieval needs an ANN side-car (Vespa, Vald, Milvus, Aerospike Vector Search, Redis Search); beava does not do retrieval, only feature serving for the ranking stage. (6) No native embedding storage — high-dimensional vectors are not a primary-key aggregation. (7) No point-in-time correctness / training-serving consistency guarantees yet (Hopsworks and Tecton make this a headline feature). (8) No multi-tenancy / no namespace ACLs — a SaaS personalization vendor cannot safely host multiple customers on one box.
competition.integration_surface: Upstream producers in this domain are heterogeneous: Kafka (large marketplaces), Kinesis (AWS-native shops), the application server's own click / impression / view webhook (HTTP push), mobile SDK direct push (for in-app dwell and scroll), gRPC from a ranking-side service. Beava's HTTP/JSON :8080 plus framed-TCP :8081 (JSON or msgpack) maps cleanly to the webhook and mobile-SDK paths; a thin Kafka/Kinesis consumer is needed for the streaming paths and is not in v0. Downstream consumers are the ranker (XGBoost / LightGBM / two-tower / cross-encoder / transformer) and an optional rules / business-logic layer (diversity, freshness, business constraints), all pulling features via batch_get inside the ranking RPC.
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: ML scorer is dominant. Most production stacks are XGBoost / LightGBM (Meesho, DoorDash, Instacart historically), increasingly two-tower retrieval + neural re-rankers (Whatnot, Pinterest, Meta) plus cross-encoder rerankers for the head queries. Rules engines are used only for hard business constraints (don't show this seller to this user, freshness cap, diversity quota). Beava sits under the ML scorer.

adoption_signals.existing_public_users_or_case_studies: No publicly named beava users running this use case yet. Comparable published case studies that legitimise the shape of the problem: Whatnot on Chalk (300M+ features/sec, ~100 ms P99, ~150 ms end-to-end with 1 MB+ payloads, thousands of livestreams ranked per session, cold-start <1 h vs prior 24 h); DoorDash on Redis (store ranking >1M predictions/sec, 23 features per prediction, >20M feature reads/sec, 38 % latency reduction after optimization); Apartment List on Chalk (query-time ranking features, sub-5 ms feature retrieval); Instacart on internal 'Griffin' platform (real-time feature store + online inference, Flink-based materialization); Myntra on Aerospike (re-ranking, feature lookup was the bottleneck before migration); Sony PlayStation on Aerospike (personalized recommendations); Meesho on XGBoost-to-DL ranking (mission-critical sub-5 ms ranking constraint). [uncertain] specific published throughput / latency numbers for Tecton / Hopsworks / Fennel production tiers.
adoption_signals.community_discussions: [uncertain] Specific beava Discord / GitHub Discussion threads on recsys / ranking — the repo ships a python/beava/demos/ecommerce/ directory with PageView / AddToCart / Purchase events keyed on user_id and sku (verified by reading schema.json), which signals e-commerce / personalization is a first-class internal use case, but external community traction in the recsys vertical specifically has not been verified through this research.
adoption_signals.examples_or_demos_in_repo: Yes — /tmp/docker-desktop-root/run/desktop/mnt/host/d/Code/Beava/beava/python/beava/demos/ecommerce/ (schema.json + events.jsonl) already ships PageView, AddToCart and Purchase events keyed on user_id / sku, which is the recsys event shape. No explicit per-item rolling-popularity or per-(user, category) affinity demo was found; that would be a natural extension. [uncertain] whether crates/beava-bench ships a recsys-shaped workload analogous to the fraud-team.json workload.
adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: Passive load. Personalization / ranking has no active adversary in the fraud / anti-cheat sense — no one is trying to make the feature server return wrong values. Feature drift is driven by genuine user-behaviour shifts (seasonality, trends, viral events) rather than by an adversary, which means feature-staleness tolerances are more forgiving than in fraud. The exception is integrity / ranking-manipulation (sellers gaming popularity counters), which exists but is handled by separate trust-and-safety logic, not by the feature store.

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: Beava is the wrong tool for: (1) Candidate retrieval / first-stage ANN (millions-to-thousands narrowing) — that needs a vector index (Vespa, Milvus, Vald, Aerospike Vector Search, Redis Search) and is not a primary-key counter problem. (2) Long historical training-data materialization with point-in-time correctness — that belongs in a warehouse (Snowflake Dynamic Tables, Databricks, BigQuery) with Tecton / Hopsworks / Feast handling the offline-online sync. (3) Embedding storage / similarity search. (4) Joins across entities at query time (user × item joins are computed at the ranker, not in the feature store). (5) Cross-region active-active state for global platforms in v0. (6) Multi-tenant SaaS personalization platforms hosting many customers on one box.
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava would need to ship for this domain, in roughly priority order: (1) TLS + authentication (mTLS or bearer-token) on :8080/:8081 — non-negotiable before any production ranking team will let beava into their VPC. (2) batch_get fan-out optimization — a published benchmark for the (1 user × 30 user-features) + (200 items × 30 item-features) + (200 pairs × 5 pair-features) shape with target P99 < 5 ms. (3) Native last-N list primitive (LPUSH/LTRIM-like behaviour) for recently-viewed / recently-clicked / recently-purchased streams; explicitly listed as part of beava's 50+ primitives but worth verifying. (4) In-process sharding / consistent hashing across multiple beava instances for horizontal scaling. (5) Point-in-time correctness story for training-serving consistency (offline materialization that replays the same aggregation primitives over a historical event log). (6) Multi-tenancy / namespace ACLs for SaaS deployments. (7) Right-to-erasure helper (per-entity delete that propagates through all derived aggregates). (8) Kafka / Kinesis consumer side-car (not in v0; many recsys event streams sit on Kafka). (9) Optional vector / embedding sidecar — beava itself probably should not become an ANN index, but a documented integration with a vector DB closes the candidate-retrieval gap. (10) Approximate-aggregation primitives (HLL, CMS, T-Digest) for high-cardinality unique-viewer / dwell-distribution features; need to confirm coverage in beava's published 50+ primitives. (11) Triggers / 'fire when item velocity exceeds threshold' — useful for trending-now and cold-start surfacing.
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Optional but useful. Pure feature serving is sufficient for the core ranking job. Triggers (fire when an item's velocity crosses a threshold, fire when a user enters a new high-affinity category) would enable trending-now widgets and real-time cold-start surfacing, but a ranker that polls per request also works.
